analysis.one_liner: Sets national policing standards, requires stop-and-force data reporting, and funds police misconduct oversight.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 54 Democratic cosponsors, the bill never got a committee vote and died in a House Judiciary subcommittee when the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the Justice Department develop uniform accreditation standards for police departments covering use of force, civilian review, and stop-and-search procedures, and offer grants to departments that pursue accreditation. It would require every law enforcement agency to report data on traffic stops, pedestrian stops, searches, and deadly force — broken down by race, ethnicity, age, and gender — and cut federal crime funding from states that refuse. It would also fund pilot programs for civilian review boards, study rules that let officers delay misconduct interviews, and send medallions to families of officers killed in the line of duty.
analysis.who_benefits: People in communities affected by police misconduct — disproportionately Black and Latino residents — gain through national data on stops and deadly force, federal support for civilian review boards, and $25 million for Justice Department lawsuits against departments with patterns of abuse. Local and tribal police departments gain access to grants for training, hiring, and accreditation. Families of fallen officers receive memorial medallions.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Justice Department to develop uniform national accreditation standards for police agencies covering use of force, civilian review, early warning systems, stop-and-search procedures, and data transparency, and to partner with accreditation organizations to push departments to adopt them.

Requires every federal, state, and local law enforcement agency to report data on traffic stops, pedestrian stops, frisks and body searches, and uses of deadly force — broken down by race, ethnicity, age, and gender — and cuts a noncompliant state's federal law enforcement assistance until it complies.

Authorizes $25 million for Justice Department enforcement of the pattern-or-practice statute and criminal civil rights laws, including consent decrees — the main federal tool for suing police departments with systemic misconduct — plus $3.3 million for the Community Relations Service.

Sets aside 20 percent of development grant funds for community-based organizations such as the NAACP and ACLU, funds pilot civilian review boards with subpoena power, and authorizes $5 million a year for a Justice Department task force to coordinate referral of misconduct complaints.

Directs a nationwide study of laws and procedures that let officers delay answering questions from internal affairs investigators — rules that can stall misconduct investigations — with a report to Congress within two years.
Creates a memorial medallion, distributed through the National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial Fund, for the families of officers killed in the line of duty.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the programs — $28.3 million authorized for fiscal 2021 plus $5 million a year for the oversight task force. Law enforcement agencies bear the cost of collecting and reporting stop and use-of-force data, keeping records for at least four years, and pursuing accreditation, and states that do not comply lose their federal law enforcement assistance funding.

drawbacks.text: The core accountability mechanism is voluntary: accreditation is encouraged through grants and consultation rather than required, so a department that refuses to seek accreditation faces no penalty; the bill does not touch qualified immunity, chokehold bans, or other measures in the stronger House police reform bill.

The data-reporting penalty strips federal law enforcement assistance from noncompliant states, meaning a state's refusal to report could reduce crime prevention and justice funding flowing into its communities.

Most grant money flows to governments and police agencies themselves — 10 percent is reserved for professional law enforcement associations and matching-fund rules apply — so much of the funding reinforces the existing policing system rather than independent oversight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is modest — roughly $33 million in authorized spending against a multibillion-dollar policing system — but so is the enforceable benefit. The bill's strongest teeth are the mandatory nationwide data collection with a funding penalty and the $25 million for pattern-or-practice lawsuits; the rest leans on grants and voluntary accreditation, which critics of policing would call too soft and which departments could simply decline. As designed, it is a supplement to, not a substitute for, binding police reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to that committee's Crime subcommittee in May 2021, and no one ever brought it up for a vote before the term ended.

narrative.text: Sheila Jackson Lee introduced the bill on March 3, 2021 with 54 Democratic cosponsors, all in the House; no Republican signed on.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and on May 18, 2021 was referred further to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security.
No further action was ever recorded: the subcommittee and full committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill died there when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments and their associations are better off: they never faced the nationwide stop-and-force data mandate, the accreditation pressure, or the strengthened pattern-or-practice enforcement the bill would have created.

for.name: Sheila Jackson Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 54 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 54 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat.

against.name: Jerrold Nadler and the House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, sent it to the Crime subcommittee, and never scheduled a markup or vote in the two years remaining in the Congress.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Prioritized the broader George Floyd Justice in Policing Act and never advanced this companion bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, but the sponsorship was entirely one-sided: all 54 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on.

industries.industry: Local and state law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Departments would face mandatory reporting of stops, searches, and deadly force, possible loss of federal assistance for noncompliance, and pressure to accept outside accreditation — but they would also receive federal grants for training, hiring, and accreditation costs. Their institutional interest in avoiding oversight runs against the bill's accountability purpose.

industries.industry: Police unions and law enforcement associations
industries.note: The bill funds a study of procedures that let officers delay internal-affairs interviews, supports civilian review boards with subpoena power, and would consult unions while writing standards — a seat at the table, but alongside new scrutiny of officer due-process protections.

Federal grants would pay departments to get accredited by these private certifying bodies, and the Justice Department would build its standards in consultation with them — locking in their role as the gatekeepers of police quality and a new revenue stream, with no guarantee the standards have teeth.
The bill reserves 20 percent of grant funds for community-based organizations like the NAACP and ACLU and defines them as formal consulting partners in setting standards and handling complaints.
